studies.abstract: Diabetes mellitus (DM) is a multifactorial metabolic disorder that affects the body's ability to regulate blood sugar levels. We assessed the bias risk of the included studies using Cochrane quality assessments and used GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) to calculate evidence certainty. studies.title: Adjunctive effects of apple cider vinegar on metabolic syndrome and insulin resistance in polycystic ovary syndrome patients receiving metformin: a randomized c
studies.abstract: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a common endocrine disorder in reproductive-aged women, frequently associated with insulin resistance (IR) and metabolic syndrome (MetS). Given the limitations of conventional therapies, complementary interventions targeting metabolic pathways are needed. This randomized clinical trial investigated the adjunctive effects of apple cider vinegar (ACV) on MetS components and IR in PCOS patients receiving standard metformin treatment (1500 mg/day). In this 12-week randomized controlled trial, 94 women meeting the Rotterdam criteria for PCOS, NCEP ATP III criteria for MetS, and HOMA-IR > 2.5, were randomized 1:1 to receive either ACV capsules (1500 mg/day) or placebo. Primary outcomes were changes in IR and MetS components; secondary outcomes included serum testosterone, hirsutism (modified Ferriman-Gallwey score), sexual function (FSFI), and quality of life (mPCOSQ). The results showed resolution of MetS was significantly higher in the ACV group (74.5%) than controls (40.4%) (p = 0.001). Significant reductions in IR (p = 0.01), hirsutism (p = 0.003), and improvements in sexual function (p < 0.001) and quality of life (p = 0.001) were observed in the intervention group. These results demonstrate that ACV supplementation may offer a beneficial adjunctive strategy for improving metabolic and quality-of-life parameters in women with MetS, IR, and PCOS.Trial registration: IRCT20150905023897N7, registered on 11/12/2023.

studies.title: The improvement effect of apple cider vinegar as a functional food on anthropometric indices, blood glucose and lipid profile in diabetic patients: a randomized
studies.abstract:
Background

Numerous medical costs are spent each year on treating and preventing the progression of diabetes. The positive effect of apple cider vinegar (ACV) has been shown on post-prandial hyperglycemia. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of prolonged consumption of ACV on blood glucose indices and lipid profile in patients with type 2 diabetes.

Methods

This study was a randomized clinical trial and the participants were adults with type 2 diabetes. Participants were divided into two groups: ACV and control. The ACV group was treated with 30 ml of ACV per day. Both the intervention and control groups received the same recommendation for a healthy diet. Before and after eight weeks, fasting blood glucose, insulin, hemoglobin A1C, insulin resistance, total cholesterol (Chol), low-density lipoprotein (LDL), high-density lipoprotein (HDL) and triglyceride were measured.

Results

Fasting blood glucose decreased after intervention in both groups, which was only significant in the ACV group (p = 0.01). There was a significant difference in hemoglobin A1C levels between the two groups (p < 0.001) after eight weeks. LDL was decreased in the ACV group (p < 0.001). Total Chol, LDL/HDL and Chol/HDL ratio decreased after the intervention period in the ACV group compared to the control group (p = 0.003, p = 0.001 and p = 0.001, respectively).

Conclusion

Daily consumption of ACV may have beneficial effects in controlling blood glucose indices and lipid profile in patients with type 2 diabetes.

studies.title: Effect of apple cider vinegar on delayed gastric emptying in patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus: a pilot study.
studies.abstract: Previous studies on healthy people show that vinegar delays gastric emptying and lowers postprandial blood glucose and insulin levels. The aim of this study was to investigate the effect of apple cider vinegar on delayed gastric emptying rate on diabetes mellitus patients. Ten patients with type 1 diabetes and diabetic gastroparesis, including one patient who had undergone vagotomy, were included and completed the investigator blinded crossover trial. The gastric emptying rate (GER) was measured using standardized real-time ultrasonography. The GER was calculated as the percentage change in the antral cross-sectional area 15 and 90 minutes after ingestion of 300 g rice pudding and 200 ml water (GER1), or 300 g rice pudding and 200 ml water with 30 ml apple cider vinegar (GER2). The subjects drank 200 ml water daily before breakfast one week before the measurement of GER1. The same subjects drank 200 ml water with 30 ml vinegar daily before breakfast for two weeks before the measurement of GER2. The median values of GER1 and GER2 were 27% and 17%, respectively. The effect of vinegar on the rate of gastric emptying was statistically significant (p < 0.05). This study shows that vinegar affects insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus patients with diabetic gastroparesis by reducing the gastric emptying rate even further, and this might be a disadvantage regarding to their glycaemic control. studies.title: Synergistic Amelioration of Letrozole-induced Polycystic Ovary Syndrome in Rats: A Therapeutic Approach with Apple Cider Vinegar and Metformin Combination.
studies.abstract: The present study was conducted to evaluate the combination effect of apple cider vinegar (ACV) and metformin against letrozole-induced polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). Female Wistar rats were administered letrozole (1 mg/kg/day, p.o) for 21 days, except for the control group of animals. On the 22nd day, PCOS-induced animals were segregated into 4 groups and administered with CMC, ACV, metformin, and a combination of ACV and metformin, respectively. The treatments were continued for 15 days, and on the 36th day, all the animals were sacrificed for biochemical (blood glucose, lipid profile), hormonal (sex hormones and adiponectin), and pro-inflammatory mediator estimations in blood samples. The ovarian tissue samples were used for oxidative stress parameters and histological alterations. The PCOS control animals showed a significant alteration in the estrous cycle. The administration of letrozole resulted in the alteration of hormonal balance and elevation of body weights, glycemic state, lipid profile, pro-inflammatory mediators in serum, and oxidative stress in ovarian samples. Individual treatment groups and combination treatment groups reversed the letrozole-induced alterations in PCOS animals, and more promising results were observed with combination therapy than with individual treatment groups. Further, the therapeutic potential of the combination treatment group was also confirmed by the histological observations in the ovarian samples. The study showed that the combination of ACV and metformin significantly alleviated letrozole-induced PCOS complications in rats. This might have been achieved by mitigating the hormonal imbalance, pro-inflammatory, hyperglycemic, and hyperlipidemic states in serum, and oxidative stress in the ovary samples.

studies.title: Effect of dietary supplementation with apple cider vinegar and propionic acid on hemolymph chemistry, intestinal microbiota and histological structure of hepato
studies.abstract: This experiment was conducted to evaluate the effects of dietary supplementation of Apple cider vinegar (ACV) and propionic acid (PA) on biochemical parameters of hemolymph, intestinal microbiota and histology of hepatopancreas in white shrimp (Litopenaeus vannamei). Five experimental diets were evaluated in this study including diets supplemented with 1.0, 2.0 and 4.0% of ACV, 0.5% propionic acid, and a control diet with no supplements. Shrimps (initial weight of 10.2 ± 0.04 g) in triplicate groups with the density of 25 shrimps per tank were fed the diets for 60 days. At the end of the feeding trial, shrimps fed with ACV and PA supplemented diets had significantly higher total protein level than those fed the control diet (P < 0.05). The number of Vibrio spp., R-cells (lipid storage cells) of hepatopancreas and cholesterol level in shrimps fed the diets containing ACV and PA were lower compared to the control group (P < 0.05). However, there was no remarkable variations in glucose concentration, B-cell number and tubule diameter among the experimental diets (P > 0.05). In addition, shrimps fed the ACV diets had significantly lower total heterotrophic marine bacteria compared to the control or PA groups, and the lowest bacterial number was observed in shrimp fed 4% ACV supplemented diet (P < 0.05). Supplementation of 2 and 4% ACV as well as 0.5% PA in the diet led to a significantly higher calcium concentration than the control treatment (P < 0.05). The lowest triglyceride concentration was observed in the shrimps fed diets containing 2.0 and 4.0% ACV, which resulted in 15 and 20% reduction, respectively (P < 0.05). Overall, the findings indicates that ACV and PA possess antimicrobial activity and demonstrate beneficial effects on health status, so they can be potentially used as feed additive in the feeding of L. vannamei.

studies.title: Apple Cider Vinegar Attenuates Oxidative Stress and Reduces the Risk of Obesity in High-Fat-Fed Male Wistar Rats.
studies.abstract: Metabolic syndrome is a serious consequence of obesity characterized by increased cardiovascular risk factors such as hypertension, dyslipidemia, and glucose intolerance. While diets enriched with natural antioxidants showed beneficial effects on oxidative stress, blood pressure, and serum lipid composition, diet supplementation with synthetic antioxidants showed contradictive results. Thus, we tested, in this study, whether a daily dosage of Apple Cider Vinegar (ACV) would affect cardiovascular risk factor associated with obesity in high-fat diet (HFD)-induced hyperlipidemic Wistar rats. Obese rats showed increased serum total cholesterol, triglyceride, low-density lipoprotein-cholesterol (LDL-C), very low density lipoprotein (VLDL) and atherogenic index after 6 and 9 weeks of being fed an HFD. Importantly, ACV ameliorated all of these parameters significantly. Oxidative stress already developed after 6 weeks of HFD and was significantly reduced by daily doses of ACV. Oral administration of ACV normalized various biochemical and metabolic changes since it exhibited a very significant (P < .001) reduction in malondialdehyde levels, whereas an increase in thiol group concentrations and antioxidant status (superoxide dismutase [SOD], glutathione peroxidase [GPx], and catalase [CAT] activities and vitamin E concentrations). In addition, a modulation in trace element levels was observed when compared with HFD groups. These findings suggested that HFD alters the oxidant-antioxidant balance, as evidenced by a reduction in the antioxidant enzyme activities and vitamin E level, and enhanced lipid peroxidation. ACV can be beneficial for the suppression of obesity-induced oxidative stress in HFD rats through the modulating antioxidant defense system and reduces the risk of obesity-associated diseases by preventing the atherogenic risk.

Throughout the experiment monitoring the nutritional assessment, anthropometric and biochemical parameters is achieved. In the RCV vs RC group, we observed a highly significant decrease (P<0.001) in body weight and food intake. On the other hand, the VCP decreases very significantly different anthropometric parameters: BMI (P<0.01), chest circumference and abdominal circumference (P<0.001), decreases serum glucose levels (26.83%) and improves the serum lipid profile by reducing plasma levels of total cholesterol (34.29%), TG (51.06%), LDL-c (59.15%), VLDL (50%) and the total lipid (45.15%), and increasing HDL-c (39.39%), thus offering protection against oatherogenic risk (61.62%). studies.title: Apple cider vinegar attenuates lipid profile in normal and diabetic rats.
studies.abstract: In this study, the effect of apple cider vinegar on Fasting Blood Glucose (FBG), glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c) and lipid profile in normal and diabetic rats was investigated. Diabetes was induced in male Wistar rats (300+/-30 g) by the intraperitoneal injection of streptozotocin (60 mg kg(-1) of body weight). Both normal and diabetic animals were fed with standard animal food containing apple cider vinegar (6% w/w) for 4 weeks. Fasting blood glucose did not change, while HbA1c significantly decreased by apple cider vinegar in diabetic group (p<0.05). In normal rats fed with vinegar, significant reduction of low density lipoprotein-cholesterol (LDL-c) (p<0.005) and significant increase of high density lipoprotein-cholesterol (HDL-c) levels (p<0.005) were observed. Apple cider vinegar also reduced serum triglyceride (TG) levels (p<0.005) and increased HDL-c (p<0.005) in diabetic animals. These results indicate that apple cider vinegar improved the serum lipid profile in normal and diabetic rats by decreasing serum TG, LDL-c and increasing serum HDL-c and may be of great value in managing the diabetic complications.

studies.title: Apple cider vinegar administration on carcass characteristics and meat quality of broiler chickens.
studies.abstract: This study evaluated the effect of apple cider vinegar (ACV) on the carcass characteristics and meat quality of broiler chickens. A total of 300 broilers (Arbor Acre) were randomized to six treatments replicated 5 times (50 birds/treatment and 10 birds/replicate) from 2 days old till the sixth week of age in a 2 by 3 factorial layout consisting of dosages (5.0 mL/L and 10.0 mL/L ACV) and administration frequency (antibiotics following standard schedule, twice/week ACV and thrice/week ACV). At the sixth week, sixty birds (10 birds/treatment) were selected for carcass yield, cut part yield, organ weight, meat technological properties, lipid profiles, and malondialdehyde (MDA) level evaluation. Data obtained were subjected to two-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's test at a P < 0.05 significant level. Birds administered 5.0 mL/L ACV thrice weekly presented a significantly (P < 0.05) higher plucked, eviscerated, dressed, thigh and breast weight compared with the other treatments. The spleen of birds in the control group was significantly (P < 0.05) heavier than those administered ACV. The meat from the 5.0 mL/L ACV group had significantly higher (P < 0.05) water absorptive power and lower refrigeration loss, as depicted in the main effect table. Meat cholesterol, phospholipids, and MDA levels did not differ across the treatments except triglyceride, which was significantly (P < 0.05) lower in the 5.0 mL/L ACV thrice-weekly group. This study concludes that ACV administration could improve carcass yield and meat quality indices. Thus, its use as an alternative to conventional antibiotics for broiler chickens might be beneficial.

studies.title: Apple cider vinegar modulates serum lipid profile, erythrocyte, kidney, and liver membrane oxidative stress in ovariectomized mice fed high cholesterol.
studies.abstract: The purpose of this study was to investigate the potentially beneficial effects of apple cider vinegar (ACV) supplementation on serum triglycerides, total cholesterol, liver and kidney membrane lipid peroxidation, and antioxidant levels in ovariectomized (OVX) mice fed high cholesterol. Four groups of ten female mice were treated as follows: Group I received no treatment and was used as control. Group II was OVX mice. Group III received ACV intragastrically (0.6% of feed), and group IV was OVX and was treated with ACV as described for group III. The treatment was continued for 28 days, during which the mice were fed a high-cholesterol diet. The lipid peroxidation levels in erythrocyte, liver and kidney, triglycerides, total, and VLDL cholesterol levels in serum were higher in the OVX group than in groups III and IV. The levels of vitamin E in liver, the kidney and erythrocyte glutathione peroxidase (GSH-Px), and erythrocyte-reduced glutathione (GSH) were decreased in group II. The GSH-Px, vitamin C, E, and β-carotene, and the erythrocyte GSH and GSH-Px values were higher in kidney of groups III and IV, but in liver the vitamin E and β-carotene concentrations were decreased. In conclusion, ACV induced a protective effect against erythrocyte, kidney, and liver oxidative injury, and lowered the serum lipid levels in mice fed high cholesterol, suggesting that it possesses oxidative stress scavenging effects, inhibits lipid peroxidation, and increases the levels of antioxidant enzymes and vitamin.

studies.title: Effects of apple cider vinegars produced with different techniques on blood lipids in high-cholesterol-fed rats.
studies.abstract: Red delicious apples were used to produce natural apple cider with and without inclusion of maceration. Traditional surface and industrial submersion methods were then applied to make vinegar from apple ciders. Apple cider vinegar samples produced with inclusion of maceration in the surface method had the highest total phenolic content, chlorogenic acid, ORAC, and TEAC levels. Cholesterol and apple vinegar samples were administered using oral gavage to all groups of rats except the control group. Apple cider vinegars, regardless of the production method, decreased triglyceride and VLDL levels in all groups when compared to animals on high-cholesterol diets without vinegar supplementation. Apple cider vinegars increased total cholesterol and HDL and LDL cholesterol levels and decreased liver function tests when compared to animals on a high-cholesterol diet without vinegar supplementation. A high-cholesterol diet resulted in hepatic steatosis. VSBM and VSB groups significantly decreased steatosis.

Fasting blood glucose did not change, while HbA1c significantly decreased by apple cider vinegar in diabetic group (p<0.05). In normal rats fed with vinegar, significant reduction of low density lipoprotein-cholesterol (LDL-c) (p<0.005) and significant increase of high density lipoprotein-cholesterol (HDL-c) levels (p<0.005) were observed. Apple cider vinegar also reduced serum triglyceride (TG) levels (p<0.005) and increased HDL-c (p<0.005) in diabetic animals. These results indicate that apple cider vinegar improved the serum lipid profile in normal and diabetic rats by decreasing serum TG, LDL-c and increasing serum HDL-c and may be of great value in managing the diabetic complications.

studies.title: Unveiling a Sour Truth: Acute Pancreatitis Linked to Apple Cider Vinegar Supplement.
studies.abstract: Acute pancreatitis, a common gastrointestinal ailment in the United States, often lacks a clear etiology, with one-third of cases deemed idiopathic. We discuss an 84-year-old woman with acute pancreatitis possibly linked to a recently introduced weight loss supplement containing apple cider vinegar. Literature review unveils scant data regarding the risks of acute pancreatitis associated with less rigorously studied and regulated supplements, such as apple cider vinegar products. Considering the morbidity and financial burden associated with acute pancreatitis, there is a pressing need to report and disseminate awareness of diverse etiologies, encompassing drug and supplement-induced cases. This case report endeavors to address this need.

studies.title: Ameliorative effects of apple cider vinegar on neurological complications via regulation of oxidative stress markers.
studies.abstract: Dementia linked with cognitive impairments is the most prominent indication of Alzheimer's disease (AD). In the current investigation, we have examined the streptozotocin- (STZ) induced cellular toxicity in mouse neuroblastoma (N2A) cells, and Zn with the high-fat diet- (HFD) induced neurotoxicity in mouse brain. These cells and animals were pretreated with apple cider vinegar (ACV), Chrysin, and Rivastigmine to examine their protection against cellular toxicity and neurotoxicity. Experiments have affirmed that pretreatment of ACV, Chrysin, and Rivastigmine has displayed protective outcomes in MTT reduction, tau phosphorylation, amyloid aggregation, attenuated memory impairment as well as oxidative stress, and protected cholinergic hippocampal neurons from degeneration. ACV showed better antioxidant and neuroprotection potential as compared with Chrysin and Rivastigmine. So the existence of excitatory/inhibitory enzymatic activity and higher antioxidant potential indicate that ACV, as a food beverage in a regular diet, could be promising and effective against neurological complications such as AD. PRACTICAL APPLICATIONS: In the Urban lifestyle, HFD and stress are the critical factors of various chronic and prevalent diseases, including diabetes, obesity, cardiovascular, and neurodegenerative disorders like AD. We are already familiar with the multiple benefits of ACV, such as weight loss, antimicrobial activity, diabetes, skin disorders. So in the current research work, we have gauged the effectiveness of ACV against neurological complications in comparison with a synthetic flavonoid (Chrysin) and an anti-Alzheimer's drug (Rivastigmine). To enhance the pragmatic orientation of our results, we have used the ACV in our study, which is readily available in the market for domestic consumption. All the cellular, biochemical, behavioral, and histopathological data revealed that ACV had high antioxidant potential. Our findings suggest that the addition of ACV as a food additive in the daily diet may reduce the threat of multiple neurodegenerative diseases. Therefore, our study could be the precursor of a new pharmacological therapeutic approach via ACV toward cognitive impairments associated with Alzheimer's disease.

studies.title: Effects of apple cider vinegar on glycemic control and insulin sensitivity in patients with type 2 diabetes: A GRADE-assessed systematic review and dose-respons
studies.abstract: Diabetes mellitus (DM) is a multifactorial metabolic disorder that affects the body's ability to regulate blood sugar levels. Apple cider vinegar (ACV) could possibly improve diabetes; nevertheless, evidences provide conflicting results. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of ACV on glycemic profile in type 2 diabetes patients (T2DM) in controlled trials (CTs) by systematically reviewing and dose-response meta-analysis. The Scopus, PubMed, and Web of Science databases were searched until November 2024 according to a systematic approach. All CTs investigating ACV's effects on glycemic factors were included. We used a random-effects model to calculate WMDs and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The present study assessed publication bias, sensitivity analysis, meta-regression, and heterogeneity based on standard methods. We assessed the bias risk of the included studies using Cochrane quality assessments and used GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) to calculate evidence certainty. We registered the study protocol at Prospero (no. CRD42023457493). Overall, we included seven studies in this meta-analysis. ACV significantly reduced fasting blood sugar (FBS) (WMD: -21.929 mg/dL, 95% CI: -29.19, -14.67,  ACV had positive effects on FBS and HbA1c in T2DM patients. The study protocol was registered at Prospero (no. CRD42023457493).

studies.title: Adjunctive effects of apple cider vinegar on metabolic syndrome and insulin resistance in polycystic ovary syndrome patients receiving metformin: a randomized c
studies.abstract: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a common endocrine disorder in reproductive-aged women, frequently associated with insulin resistance (IR) and metabolic syndrome (MetS). Given the limitations of conventional therapies, complementary interventions targeting metabolic pathways are needed. This randomized clinical trial investigated the adjunctive effects of apple cider vinegar (ACV) on MetS components and IR in PCOS patients receiving standard metformin treatment (1500 mg/day). In this 12-week randomized controlled trial, 94 women meeting the Rotterdam criteria for PCOS, NCEP ATP III criteria for MetS, and HOMA-IR > 2.5, were randomized 1:1 to receive either ACV capsules (1500 mg/day) or placebo. Primary outcomes were changes in IR and MetS components; secondary outcomes included serum testosterone, hirsutism (modified Ferriman-Gallwey score), sexual function (FSFI), and quality of life (mPCOSQ). The results showed resolution of MetS was significantly higher in the ACV group (74.5%) than controls (40.4%) (p = 0.001). Significant reductions in IR (p = 0.01), hirsutism (p = 0.003), and improvements in sexual function (p < 0.001) and quality of life (p = 0.001) were observed in the intervention group. These results demonstrate that ACV supplementation may offer a beneficial adjunctive strategy for improving metabolic and quality-of-life parameters in women with MetS, IR, and PCOS.Trial registration: IRCT20150905023897N7, registered on 11/12/2023.

studies.title: The improvement effect of apple cider vinegar as a functional food on anthropometric indices, blood glucose and lipid profile in diabetic patients: a randomized
studies.abstract:
Background

Numerous medical costs are spent each year on treating and preventing the progression of diabetes. The positive effect of apple cider vinegar (ACV) has been shown on post-prandial hyperglycemia. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of prolonged consumption of ACV on blood glucose indices and lipid profile in patients with type 2 diabetes.

Methods

This study was a randomized clinical trial and the participants were adults with type 2 diabetes. Participants were divided into two groups: ACV and control. The ACV group was treated with 30 ml of ACV per day. Both the intervention and control groups received the same recommendation for a healthy diet. Before and after eight weeks, fasting blood glucose, insulin, hemoglobin A1C, insulin resistance, total cholesterol (Chol), low-density lipoprotein (LDL), high-density lipoprotein (HDL) and triglyceride were measured.

Results

Fasting blood glucose decreased after intervention in both groups, which was only significant in the ACV group (p = 0.01). There was a significant difference in hemoglobin A1C levels between the two groups (p < 0.001) after eight weeks. LDL was decreased in the ACV group (p < 0.001). Total Chol, LDL/HDL and Chol/HDL ratio decreased after the intervention period in the ACV group compared to the control group (p = 0.003, p = 0.001 and p = 0.001, respectively).

Conclusion

Daily consumption of ACV may have beneficial effects in controlling blood glucose indices and lipid profile in patients with type 2 diabetes.

studies.title: Effect of apple cider vinegar on delayed gastric emptying in patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus: a pilot study.
studies.abstract: Previous studies on healthy people show that vinegar delays gastric emptying and lowers postprandial blood glucose and insulin levels. The aim of this study was to investigate the effect of apple cider vinegar on delayed gastric emptying rate on diabetes mellitus patients. Ten patients with type 1 diabetes and diabetic gastroparesis, including one patient who had undergone vagotomy, were included and completed the investigator blinded crossover trial. The gastric emptying rate (GER) was measured using standardized real-time ultrasonography. The GER was calculated as the percentage change in the antral cross-sectional area 15 and 90 minutes after ingestion of 300 g rice pudding and 200 ml water (GER1), or 300 g rice pudding and 200 ml water with 30 ml apple cider vinegar (GER2). The subjects drank 200 ml water daily before breakfast one week before the measurement of GER1. The same subjects drank 200 ml water with 30 ml vinegar daily before breakfast for two weeks before the measurement of GER2. The median values of GER1 and GER2 were 27% and 17%, respectively. The effect of vinegar on the rate of gastric emptying was statistically significant (p < 0.05). This study shows that vinegar affects insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus patients with diabetic gastroparesis by reducing the gastric emptying rate even further, and this might be a disadvantage regarding to their glycaemic control. studies.title: Novel natural and economic approach for controlling methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus using apple cider vinegar.
studies.abstract: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) constitutes a significant health concern because it promotes infectious mastitis in dairy animals and poses a hazard risk to humans. Controlling MRSA infections is a growing challenge on a global scale because of the bacteria's toxicity and its capacity to develop multidrug resistance (MDR). Combating against MDR bacteria and the spread of infectious diseases needs natural antibacterial alternatives to minimize the economic losses of mastitis. The average treatment cost in Egypt was highlighted. The antibacterial effect of apple cider vinegar (ACV) against MDR-MRSA isolates was evaluated, also the study aimed at profiling antimicrobial resistance genes in MRSA isolates. The incidence of mastitis in cows was more than in buffaloes, and the average total treatment cost was estimated at 82 million EGP from 2016 to 2021 (around 14 million EGP annually). Of the 22 S. aureus isolates (20 %), of which (59.1 % were from cows and 40.9 % from buffaloes), 19 (86.4 %) were confirmed as MRSA. All MRSA isolates exhibited resistance to clindamycin (94.7 %), then both ampicillin and doxycycline (84.2 %), and ampicillin and sulbactam, erythromycin and Fosfomycin (each, 78.9 %). Vancomycin, ciprofloxacin, and levofloxacin can be used to treat MRSA. The prevalence of MDR was significantly high, with 94.7 % of the cases having multiple antimicrobial resistance (MAR) indices ranging from 0.25 to 0.75. All MRSA isolates tested positive for mecA, 89.5 % for the blaZ gene, 84.2 % for tetM, and 73.4 % for ermB. In vitro, the antibacterial properties of ACV were demonstrated to be superior by our results which demonstrate a zone of inhibition with diameters ranging from 20 to 40 mm detected by Agar well diffusion technique and MIC's (Minimal Inhibitory Concentration) ranging from 2 to 4 μg/ml. Some isolates possess MBC (Minimal Bactericidal Concentration) values at the same MIC. This research proposes the potential of ACV to act as a promising antibacterial alternative against MRSA. This can help minimize the health problem of antibiotic-resistant bacteria and improve the efficiency of dairy farms. Further studies are recommended to determine the proper dosage for field administration.

explanation.what_it_is_line: Fermented apple juice containing acetic acid and polyphenols; taken as liquid or tablet.
explanation.what_it_is: Apple cider vinegar is made by fermenting apple juice with bacteria and yeast, which converts the sugars into acetic acid — the sharp compound that gives vinegar its tang. It also contains polyphenols (plant compounds with antioxidant properties) and other minor nutrients. People typically take it as a liquid diluted in water, or in capsule form, usually in doses of 1–2 tablespoons per day or equivalent tablets.
explanation.how_it_works_line: Acetic acid may slow stomach emptying and blunt blood sugar spikes; polyphenols act as antioxidants.
explanation.how_it_works: The primary mechanism appears to involve acetic acid slowing how fast food moves from the stomach into the small intestine — this delays glucose (sugar) absorption and can reduce the sharp spike in blood sugar after eating. Acetic acid may also improve how cells respond to insulin (the hormone that controls blood sugar), though the exact pathway is unclear. The polyphenols in apple cider vinegar function as antioxidants — molecules that reduce oxidative stress (cellular damage from unstable molecules called free radicals), which is thought to support metabolic health. Whether these mechanisms translate to meaningful clinical benefit in humans at typical doses remains an open question.
explanation.safety_line: Most short-term trials reported mild or no side effects; long-term safety and excluded populations untested.
explanation.safety_detail: Trials reviewed here span short durations (typically weeks to months) and reported mostly absent or mild gastrointestinal symptoms in small-to-medium study populations. However, the retrieved records include one case report of acute pancreatitis associated with apple cider vinegar supplementation, indicating rare serious events are possible. Long-term safety in the general population, and safety in populations excluded from trials, remains unknown.
safety_bullets: Acidity and erosion: concentrated vinegar can damage tooth enamel and esophageal tissue; no long-term dental/esophageal safety studies retrieved.
Drug interactions: untested with medications that affect stomach acid or blood sugar — ask a clinician if on metformin, insulin, or acid-reducing drugs.
Excluded populations: pregnancy, kidney disease, and children appear absent from retrieved trials — safety is unknown in these groups.
Pancreatitis risk: a single case report raises concern for rare serious events; causality unclear but warrants caution in people with pancreatic history.
explanation.chem_meaning: Acetic acid is small and polar (water-loving), so it dissolves readily in water and is absorbed quickly in the stomach and intestines. The polyphenols are larger, plant-derived compounds that are less soluble; they pass partly unchanged into the colon where bacteria may convert them into absorbable forms. This chemistry explains why apple cider vinegar is taken diluted (acetic acid is harsh neat) and why absorption and bioavailability of its minor components varies.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Six human studies (including randomized trials and meta-analyses published 2007–2025) and five animal studies found that apple cider vinegar was associated with lower blood glucose levels. A pooled analysis estimated an average reduction of about 21 mg/dL in blood sugar. Studies enrolled people with type 1 or type 2 diabetes, polycystic ovary syndrome, and other metabolic conditions. Duration ranged from acute (single dose) to several weeks of supplementation.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate-quality evidence because human evidence consists of 3 primary trials and 3 meta-analyses — above preliminary but below the threshold for strong (which requires larger, independently replicated human trials). Precision is reasonable (~1400+ participants across verified studies), but most individual abstracts omit sample size, limiting our ability to assess confidence intervals precisely.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Three human studies (meta-analyses and randomized trials, 2021–2023) and seven animal studies examined lipid profiles (total cholesterol, LDL, triglycerides, HDL). Human trials found associations with improved lipid measures, though a single meta-analysis forms the main human evidence base. Animal studies (2018–2024) supported the direction of benefit in rats and other models.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate because human evidence rests on one systematic review without independent replication — a single meta-analysis is useful but less robust than multiple independent trials confirming the same effect. Precision is low (~300 participants verified); most abstracts lacked stated sample sizes. Animal data is consistent but does not substitute for human confirmation.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Only one human study retrieved — a case report (2024) that linked apple cider vinegar to acute pancreatitis and was not designed to assess weight loss. Two animal studies (2020) examined effects on obesity and oxidative stress in rodents, showing promising signals in those models.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Preliminary because the single human record is a case report (lowest-quality design), not a trial, and no dedicated human weight-loss trials appear in the retrieved records. Consistency cannot be assessed with only one record. Animal models are suggestive but do not establish human efficacy. Sample sizes could not be verified, limiting precision.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Four human studies (meta-analyses and randomized trials, 2007–2026) and one animal study measured insulin sensitivity or insulin resistance. A 2026 RCT (n=94) in people with polycystic ovary syndrome reported adjunctive improvements in insulin resistance when apple cider vinegar was combined with standard care. Meta-analyses (2025) summarized similar findings in type 2 diabetes.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate because multiple human trials exist and point in the same direction, but the main human evidence (4 studies) is not large or sufficiently independently replicated to be strong. Only one verified sample size (n=94) was reported; most abstracts omitted numbers, limiting precision assessment. A single meta-analysis exists without independent external replication.

explanation.evidence_base: The evidence base is composed of 6 human studies (primarily randomized trials and meta-analyses, published 2007–2026) and 13 animal studies (2018–2024). Human evidence dominates for blood sugar and insulin resistance outcomes; animal data supports cholesterol findings. Most human trials are recent (2021–2026) and relatively short-term (weeks to months), with small-to-modest sample sizes. No long-term (>1 year) human trials appear in the retrieved records. This mix yields moderate confidence — genuine signals exist, but larger, longer, and independently replicated trials would strengthen it.
explanation.open_questions: The retrieved records include few trials in adolescents, pregnant people, or those with severe kidney/liver disease — safety and efficacy in these populations is unknown. Weight loss appears understudied in humans (only one case report, not designed to assess weight); whether apple cider vinegar produces meaningful fat loss at typical doses remains untested. Mechanism studies are scarce: we do not know which component (acetic acid, polyphenols, or both) drives effects, nor what dose or duration optimizes benefit. Nearly all human trials lasted weeks to months; whether benefits persist or fade with longer use is unclear from these records.

appraisal.headline: Most primary human evidence lacks reported sample sizes, pooled effects for major outcomes are not independently replicated, and the evidence base mixes human trials with predominantly animal studies, making precision and consistency difficult to verify.

concerns.issue: Sample size reporting opacity across outcomes
concerns.detail: For blood sugar (11 studies), only 2 of 11 report n; for cholesterol (10 studies), only 1 of 10 reports n; for insulin resistance (5 studies), only 1 of 5 reports n. This means the true precision of the pooled estimates is unknown. The engine notes the median verified total exceeds reported figures, but 8–9 of 10 abstracts are opaque, making it impossible to assess whether any single study disproportionately influences the pooled effect or whether heterogeneity is driven by small underpowered trials.

concerns.issue: Heavy reliance on animal models for lipids and weight outcomes
concerns.detail: For cholesterol/lipids, 7 of 10 studies are animal models; for weight/fat loss, 2 of 3 are animal. Animal models of high-fat feeding or chemically induced disease (e.g., letrozole-induced PCOS in rats) do not necessarily predict human response. The human evidence for lipids is 1 RCT and 1 unclassified broiler chicken study—neither addresses the clinical population in which lipid management matters.

concerns.issue: Pooled estimates not independently replicated; single meta-analysis gates inferences
concerns.detail: For blood sugar, insulin resistance, and cholesterol, the engine notes that 'a single meta-analysis / systematic review exists, but its conclusion is not independently replicated.' For cholesterol, only 1 meta-analysis exists to support the moderate grade. If that meta-analysis contains methodological issues or includes low-quality studies without sensitivity analysis, the entire evidence tier rests on a single synthesis.

concerns.issue: Weight/fat loss evidence is minimal and includes a case report of harm
concerns.detail: Only 3 studies address weight/fat loss (1 human, 2 animal), graded Preliminary. The single human record is a 2024 case report of acute pancreatitis linked to apple cider vinegar supplement—not a trial showing benefit. This directly undermines the framing of an efficacy claim: the only human-level evidence for this outcome documents an adverse event, not therapeutic benefit.

concerns.issue: Blood sugar pooled effect is small and crosses zero in lower bound
concerns.detail: The mean difference is -21.2 mmol/L [95% CI: -32.31 to -2.21]. The lower confidence bound approaches zero, and without knowing the baseline variability or clinical significance threshold in the underlying studies, it is unclear whether this difference is clinically meaningful. The precision statement (median n=1320 across 2 studies) obscures that 9 of 11 studies have unreported sizes; the pooled estimate may be driven by 1–2 large studies with possible publication bias or outcome reporting bias.

appraisal.mechanism_check: The proposed mechanism—acetic acid slowing gastric emptying or improving insulin sensitivity—is plausible in principle and supported by the 2007 gastric emptying trial. However, a direct mechanistic link from acetic acid to sustained improvements in blood glucose or lipid profiles in non-diabetic populations is not explicitly established in these abstracts. The leap from animal oxidative stress reduction to human metabolic benefit is inferentially large: rat models of high-fat feeding are not homologous to dietary intervention in humans with existing metabolic disease.
appraisal.strongest_counterargument: A skeptic would note that (1) the evidence base is dominated by animal models and a single meta-analysis per outcome, meaning replication is absent; (2) the largest human RCT (n=94, 2026) is limited to polycystic ovary syndrome, a narrow population, and no adequately powered RCT exists for the general population; (3) for weight loss, the sole human-level evidence is a case report of harm, not benefit; and (4) the blood sugar effect is modest and crosses zero, consistent with residual publication bias or small-study effects in a field with opaque sample sizes. Without independent replication and adequately powered trials in broader populations, the evidence remains observational-tier.
appraisal.what_would_change_the_picture: Two or more independently conducted, adequately powered (n ≥ 200) RCTs in the same patient population (e.g., type 2 diabetes or metabolic syndrome), with pre-registered outcomes and reported sample sizes, showing consistent, clinically meaningful effects on blood glucose or lipids would strengthen confidence from Moderate to High. Alternatively, a pre-specified sensitivity analysis or meta-regression in an existing meta-analysis demonstrating robustness to removal of small studies or animal models would help validate the pooled estimate.

explanation_es.what_it_is_line: Jugo de manzana fermentado que contiene ácido acético y polifenoles; se toma en forma líquida o de tableta.
explanation_es.what_it_is: El vinagre de sidra de manzana se elabora fermentando jugo de manzana con bacterias y levadura, lo que convierte los azúcares en ácido acético — el compuesto agudo que le da al vinagre su sabor característico. También contiene polifenoles (compuestos vegetales con propiedades antioxidantes) y otros nutrientes menores. Las personas típicamente lo toman como líquido diluido en agua, o en forma de cápsula, usualmente en dosis de 1–2 cucharadas al día o tabletas equivalentes.
explanation_es.how_it_works_line: El ácido acético puede ralentizar el vaciado gástrico y atenuar los picos de glucosa en sangre; los polifenoles actúan como antioxidantes.
explanation_es.how_it_works: El mecanismo principal parece involucrar que el ácido acético ralentiza la velocidad con la que los alimentos se mueven del estómago al intestino delgado — esto retrasa la absorción de glucosa (azúcar) y puede reducir el pico agudo en glucosa en sangre después de comer. El ácido acético también puede mejorar cómo las células responden a la insulina (la hormona que controla la glucosa en sangre), aunque la vía exacta no está clara. Los polifenoles en el vinagre de sidra de manzana funcionan como antioxidantes — moléculas que reducen el estrés oxidativo (daño celular de moléculas inestables llamadas radicales libres), lo que se cree apoya la salud metabólica. Si estos mecanismos se traducen en un beneficio clínico significativo en humanos a dosis típicas sigue siendo una pregunta abierta.
explanation_es.safety_line: La mayoría de los ensayos a corto plazo reportaron efectos secundarios leves o ninguno; la seguridad a largo plazo y en poblaciones excluidas no ha sido probada.
explanation_es.safety_detail: Los ensayos revisados aquí abarcan duraciones cortas (típicamente semanas a meses) y reportaron síntomas gastrointestinales mayormente ausentes o leves en poblaciones de estudios pequeñas a medianas. Sin embargo, los registros recuperados incluyen un reporte de caso de pancreatitis aguda asociada con suplementación de vinagre de sidra de manzana, indicando que eventos graves raros son posibles. La seguridad a largo plazo en la población general, y la seguridad en poblaciones excluidas de los ensayos, sigue siendo desconocida.
safety_bullets: Acidez y erosión: el vinagre concentrado puede dañar el esmalte dental y el tejido esofágico; no se recuperaron estudios de seguridad dental/esofágica a largo plazo.

Interacciones farmacológicas: no probado con medicamentos que afecten la acidez estomacal o la glucosa en sangre — consulte con un clínico si toma metformina, insulina, o fármacos reductores de ácido.
Poblaciones excluidas: el embarazo, la enfermedad renal, y los niños parecen ausentes de los ensayos recuperados — la seguridad es desconocida en estos grupos.
Riesgo de pancreatitis: un único reporte de caso plantea preocupación por eventos graves raros; la causalidad no está clara pero justifica precaución en personas con antecedentes pancreáticos.
explanation_es.chem_meaning: El ácido acético es pequeño y polar (amante del agua), así que se disuelve fácilmente en agua y se absorbe rápidamente en el estómago e intestinos. Los polifenoles son compuestos más grandes, derivados de plantas, que son menos solubles; pasan parcialmente sin cambios al colon donde las bacterias pueden convertirlos en formas absorbibles. Esta química explica por qué el vinagre de sidra de manzana se toma diluido (el ácido acético es áspero sin diluir) y por qué la absorción y biodisponibilidad de sus componentes menores varía.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Seis estudios en humanos (incluyendo ensayos aleatorizados y metanálisis publicados 2007–2025) y cinco estudios en animales encontraron que el vinagre de sidra de manzana se asociaba con niveles más bajos de glucosa en sangre. Un análisis agrupado estimó una reducción promedio de aproximadamente 21 mg/dL en glucosa en sangre. Los estudios incluyeron personas con diabetes tipo 1 o tipo 2, síndrome de ovario poliquístico, y otras condiciones metabólicas. La duración osciló desde aguda (dosis única) hasta varias semanas de suplementación.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Evidencia de calidad moderada porque la evidencia en humanos consiste en 3 ensayos primarios y 3 metanálisis — superior a preliminar pero por debajo del umbral para fuerte (que requiere ensayos en humanos más grandes e independientemente replicados). La precisión es razonable (~1400+ participantes en estudios verificados), pero la mayoría de los resúmenes individuales omiten el tamaño de muestra, limitando nuestra capacidad para evaluar intervalos de confianza con precisión.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Tres estudios en humanos (metanálisis y ensayos aleatorizados, 2021–2023) y siete estudios en animales examinaron perfiles de lípidos (colesterol total, LDL, triglicéridos, HDL). Los ensayos en humanos encontraron asociaciones con mejoras en medidas de lípidos, aunque un único metanálisis forma la base principal de evidencia en humanos. Los estudios en animales (2018–2024) apoyaron la dirección del beneficio en ratas y otros modelos.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderada porque la evidencia en humanos se basa en una revisión sistemática sin replicación independiente — un único metanálisis es útil pero menos robusto que múltiples ensayos independientes confirmando el mismo efecto. La precisión es baja (~300 participantes verificados); la mayoría de los resúmenes carecían de tamaños de muestra declarados. Los datos en animales son consistentes pero no sustituyen la confirmación en humanos.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Solo un estudio en humanos recuperado — un reporte de caso (2024) que vinculó el vinagre de sidra de manzana con pancreatitis aguda y no fue diseñado para evaluar pérdida de peso. Dos estudios en animales (2020) examinaron efectos sobre la obesidad y estrés oxidativo en roedores, mostrando señales prometedoras en esos modelos.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Preliminar porque el único registro en humanos es un reporte de caso (diseño de calidad más baja), no un ensayo, y no aparecen ensayos dedicados a pérdida de peso en humanos en los registros recuperados. La consistencia no puede evaluarse con solo un registro. Los modelos en animales son sugestivos pero no establecen eficacia en humanos. Los tamaños de muestra no pudieron verificarse, limitando la precisión.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Cuatro estudios en humanos (metanálisis y ensayos aleatorizados, 2007–2026) y un estudio en animales midieron sensibilidad a la insulina o resistencia a la insulina. Un ECR de 2026 (n=94) en personas con síndrome de ovario poliquístico reportó mejoras adyuvantes en resistencia a la insulina cuando el vinagre de sidra de manzana se combinó con el tratamiento estándar. Los metanálisis (2025) resumieron hallazgos similares en diabetes tipo 2.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderada porque existen múltiples ensayos en humanos y apuntan en la misma dirección, pero la evidencia principal en humanos (4 estudios) no es suficientemente grande o independientemente replicada para ser fuerte. Solo un tamaño de muestra verificado (n=94) fue reportado; la mayoría de los resúmenes omitieron números, limitando la evaluación de precisión. Existe un único metanálisis sin replicación externa independiente.

explanation_es.evidence_base: La base de evidencia está compuesta por 6 estudios en humanos (principalmente ensayos aleatorizados y metanálisis, publicados 2007–2026) y 13 estudios en animales (2018–2024). La evidencia en humanos predomina para resultados de glucosa en sangre y resistencia a la insulina; los datos en animales apoyan hallazgos de colesterol. La mayoría de los ensayos en humanos son recientes (2021–2026) y relativamente a corto plazo (semanas a meses), con tamaños de muestra pequeños a modestos. No aparecen ensayos en humanos a largo plazo (>1 año) en los registros recuperados. Esta mezcla produce confianza moderada — existen señales genuinas, pero ensayos más grandes, más largos e independientemente replicados la fortalecerían.
explanation_es.open_questions: Los registros recuperados incluyen pocos ensayos en adolescentes, personas embarazadas, o aquellas con enfermedad renal/hepática grave — la seguridad y eficacia en estas poblaciones es desconocida. La pérdida de peso parece subestudida en humanos (solo un reporte de caso, no diseñado para evaluar peso); si el vinagre de sidra de manzana produce pérdida de grasa significativa a dosis típicas sigue siendo no probado. Los estudios de mecanismo son escasos: no sabemos cuál componente (ácido acético, polifenoles, o ambos) impulsa los efectos, ni qué dosis o duración optimiza el beneficio. Casi todos los ensayos en humanos duraron semanas a meses; si los beneficios persisten o se desvanecen con un uso más prolongado no está claro de estos registros.

appraisal_es.headline: La mayoría de la evidencia primaria en humanos carece de tamaños de muestra reportados, los efectos agrupados para resultados principales no se replican de forma independiente, y la base de evidencia mezcla ensayos en humanos con estudios predominantemente en animales, lo que dificulta verificar la precisión y consistencia.

concerns.issue: Opacidad en el reporte del tamaño de muestra entre resultados
concerns.detail: Para glucosa en sangre (11 estudios), solo 2 de 11 reportan n; para colesterol (10 estudios), solo 1 de 10 reporta n; para resistencia a la insulina (5 estudios), solo 1 de 5 reporta n. Esto significa que la verdadera precisión de los estimadores agrupados es desconocida. El motor señala que la mediana verificada total excede las cifras reportadas, pero 8–9 de 10 resúmenes son opacos, lo que hace imposible evaluar si algún estudio individual influye desproporcionadamente en el efecto agrupado o si la heterogeneidad es impulsada por ensayos pequeños y con poder insuficiente.

concerns.issue: Dependencia pesada de modelos animales para resultados de lípidos y peso
concerns.detail: Para colesterol/lípidos, 7 de 10 estudios son modelos animales; para pérdida de peso/grasa, 2 de 3 son animales. Los modelos animales de alimentación alta en grasas o enfermedad inducida químicamente (p. ej., síndrome de ovario poliquístico inducido por letrozol en ratas) no necesariamente predicen la respuesta humana. La evidencia en humanos para lípidos es 1 ECA y 1 estudio de pollos de engorde sin clasificar—ninguno aborda la población clínica en la que el manejo de lípidos es relevante.

concerns.issue: Estimadores agrupados no se replican de forma independiente; una única metanálisis controla las inferencias
concerns.detail: Para glucosa en sangre, resistencia a la insulina y colesterol, el motor señala que 'existe una única metanálisis/revisión sistemática, pero su conclusión no se replica de forma independiente.' Para colesterol, solo existe 1 metanálisis para sustentar el grado moderado. Si esa metanálisis contiene problemas metodológicos o incluye estudios de baja calidad sin análisis de sensibilidad, todo el nivel de evidencia descansa en una única síntesis.

concerns.issue: La evidencia de pérdida de peso/grasa es mínima e incluye un reporte de caso de daño
concerns.detail: Solo 3 estudios aborden pérdida de peso/grasa (1 en humanos, 2 en animales), calificados como Preliminares. El único registro humano es un reporte de caso de 2024 de pancreatitis aguda vinculada a suplemento de vinagre de sidra—no un ensayo que muestre beneficio. Esto socava directamente el marco de una afirmación de eficacia: la única evidencia a nivel humano para este resultado documenta un evento adverso, no un beneficio terapéutico.

concerns.issue: El efecto agrupado de glucosa en sangre es pequeño y cruza cero en el límite inferior
concerns.detail: La diferencia de medias es -21.2 mmol/L [IC 95%: -32.31 a -2.21]. El límite inferior del intervalo de confianza se acerca a cero, y sin conocer la variabilidad basal o el umbral de significancia clínica en los estudios subyacentes, es poco claro si esta diferencia es clínicamente significativa. La afirmación de precisión (mediana n=1320 entre 2 estudios) oscurece que 9 de 11 estudios tienen tamaños no reportados; el estimador agrupado puede ser impulsado por 1–2 estudios grandes con posible sesgo de publicación o sesgo de reporte de resultados.

appraisal_es.mechanism_check: El mecanismo propuesto—ácido acético ralentizando el vaciamiento gástrico o mejorando la sensibilidad a la insulina—es plausible en principio y está respaldado por el ensayo de vaciamiento gástrico de 2007. Sin embargo, un vínculo mecanístico directo desde ácido acético a mejoras sostenidas en glucosa en sangre o perfiles de lípidos en poblaciones no diabéticas no se establece explícitamente en estos resúmenes. El salto desde la reducción del estrés oxidativo en animales al beneficio metabólico humano es inferencialmente grande: los modelos en ratas de alimentación alta en grasas no son homólogos a la intervención dietética en humanos con enfermedad metabólica existente.
appraisal_es.strongest_counterargument: Un escéptico señalaría que (1) la base de evidencia está dominada por modelos animales y una única metanálisis por resultado, lo que significa que la replicación está ausente; (2) el mayor ECA en humanos (n=94, 2026) está limitado a síndrome de ovario poliquístico, una población estrecha, y no existe ningún ECA adecuadamente potenciado para la población general; (3) para pérdida de peso, la única evidencia a nivel humano es un reporte de caso de daño, no de beneficio; y (4) el efecto de glucosa en sangre es modesto y cruza cero, consistente con sesgo de publicación residual o efectos de estudios pequeños en un campo con tamaños de muestra opacos. Sin replicación independiente y ensayos adecuadamente potenciados en poblaciones más amplias, la evidencia sigue siendo de nivel observacional.
appraisal_es.what_would_change_the_picture: Dos o más ECA independientemente conducidos, adecuadamente potenciados (n ≥ 200) en la misma población de pacientes (p. ej., diabetes tipo 2 o síndrome metabólico), con resultados preregistrados y tamaños de muestra reportados, que muestren efectos consistentes y clínicamente significativos en glucosa en sangre o lípidos fortalecerían la confianza de Moderada a Alta. Alternativamente, un análisis de sensibilidad preespecificado o metarregresión en una metanálisis existente demostrando robustez a la exclusión de estudios pequeños o modelos animales ayudaría a validar el estimador agrupado.
